question: Since the middle of last month, millions of plastic pellets have been washing up on Galician beaches after the Toconao (flying a flag of convenience) jettisoned part of its cargo.

Although the Galician emergency services reported the first dumping on 13 December, the Xunta’s (Galician government’s) authorities activated an anti-pollution plan 23 days later and continue to deny the seriousness of the incident, despite alerts from the entire scientific community as to the risk to human health.
Its initial failure to act, subsequent irresponsible procrastination and unambitious contingency plan may mean that much of the damage caused by the incident is already irreversible. 1.
Is the Commission aware of the ongoing environmental emergency off the coast of Galicia and of the health risks caused by the dumping of pellets?

Does it intend to demand explanations from the Galician authorities for its delay of more than 23 days in responding and the limited scope of its action, given the Galician authorities' irresponsible downplaying of the situation?
Given the impact which this may have had on Natura 2000 protected areas, does the Commission intend to open an investigation into the Galician authorities’ negligence?
answer: Subject: Dumping of microplastics in Galicia as the Galician government stands idly by A tide of plastic pellets has been washing up on the Galician coast since mid-December.

This is nothing new, as an estimated 52 000-184 000 tonnes of this material are dumped each year, but the inaction of the Xunta (autonomous government) of Galicia and its downplaying of the problem has compounded the effects of this particular spill, thus, as the Commission has recognised, jeopardising biodiversity and human health.

The recently submitted proposal for a regulation on preventing plastic pellet losses, part of the EU Plastics Strategy, the Circular Economy Action Plan and the Zero Pollution Action Plan, comes in response to this problem. However, given the particularly serious incidents we have seen, such as those in Galicia: 1.

Does the Commission believe that the exemptions and derogations the proposal grants to certain companies and treatment plants enable serious reductions to be made to existing pollution and its effects on ecosystems and human health?
Is the Commission considering intervening given the regional authorities' inaction in this particular case?

to the Commission Manu Pineda (The Left) (10 January 2024) Subject: Serious environmental and health risks caused by the Galician government’s inaction on plastic pellet dumping Since the middle of last month, millions of plastic pellets have been washing up on Galician beaches after the Toconao (flying a flag of convenience) jettisoned part of its cargo.

Although the Galician emergency services reported the first dumping on 13 December, the Xunta’s (Galician government’s) authorities activated an anti-pollution plan 23 days later and continue to deny the seriousness of the incident, despite alerts from the entire scientific community as to the risk to human health.

Its initial failure to act, subsequent irresponsible procrastination and unambitious contingency plan may mean that much of the damage caused by the incident is already irreversible. 1. Is the Commission aware of the ongoing environmental emergency off the coast of Galicia and of the health risks caused by the dumping of pellets? 2.

Does it intend to demand explanations from the Galician authorities for its delay of more than 23 days in responding and the limited scope of its action, given the Galician authorities' irresponsible downplaying of the situation? 3. Given the impact which this may have had on Natura 2000 protected areas, does the Commission intend to open an investigation into the Galician authorities’ negligence?

Joint answer given by Mr Sinkevičius on behalf of the European Commission (29 February 2024) The pollution caused by the loss of plastic pellets at every stage of the supply chain is a source of negative environmental and economic impacts and can be addressed by effective measures.

Therefore, in October 2023, the Commission adopted a legislative proposal to prevent plastic pellet losses (2), currently under examination by the European Parliament and the Council. It covers installations handling pellets at every stage of the supply chain, as well as EU and non-EU road, rail and inland waterways carriers. Lighter requirements apply to micro and small enterprises.

The pollution caused by the loss of containers shipping plastic pellets off the Portuguese coast in December 2023 raised the need for measures tackling maritime transport. The ongoing legislative process provides the possibility to consider the inclusion of further provisions in EU law, based on developments at the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) (3).

As numerous containers are loaded in non-EU ports and transported on vessels flying third-country flags, global solutions are essential. The Commission is determined, with the support of the Member States, to speed up work in IMO to ensure safe carriage of pellets by sea. Furthermore, the EU Maritime Safety Agency (4) system allows Member States to share information on containers lost at sea (5).

It was duly activated in the context of the incident on 8 December 2023. The Commission does not exercise any investigation powers in this matter as it falls under national competence. An investigation may be performed by Portugal and/or Spain under Directive 2009/18/EC (6) but as this incident would not qualify as a ‘very serious marine casualty’ such an investigation is not mandatory.

To date, the Commission is not aware of any actions taken by either Portugal or Spain under this directive in relation to this incident. Directive 2004/35/EC (7) requires that operators that have caused damage to species and habitats protected under EU law as the Birds (8) and Habitats (9) Directives, including when carrying out non-dangerous activities, such as transport of pellets, bear remedial costs.

The Commission has no information on the potential impact of this incident on Natura 2000 sites. Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, Member States authorities are primarily responsible for the correct implementation of EU law. The EU Solidarity Fund (EUSF) (10) can only be activated at the request of an eligible State affected by a natural disaster. Damages due to the liability of a third party cannot be funded by EUSF.

Council Regulation (EC) No 2012/2002 of 11 November 2002 establishing the European Union Solidarity Fund, OJ L 311, 14.11.2002, p. 3, as amended by Regulation (EU) No 661/2014 of the European Parliament and the Council of 15 May 2014, OJ L 189, 27.6.2014, p. 143 and by Regulation (EU) 2020/461 of the European Parliament and the Council of 30 March 2020, OJ L 99, 31.3.2020, p. 9.
